state_background_check.value: No — South Dakota disqualifies felons from voting (restorable by law) and can remove a sitting official convicted of certain crimes from an office they already hold, but no provision found bars someone from becoming a candidate for office in the first place; and the U.S. Constitution's own qualifications for Congress (age, citizenship, residency) can't be added to by any state regardless
state_background_check.snippet: Art. VII, § 2. Voter qualification. Every United States citizen eighteen years of age or older who has met all residency and registration requirements shall be entitled to vote in all elections and upon all questions submitted to the voters of the state unless disqualified by law for mental incompetence or the conviction of a felony. SDCL 3-4-1: An office becomes vacant if one of the following events applies to a member of a governing body or elected officer before the expiration of the term of the office; the person: ... (6) Is convicted of any infamous crime or of any offense involving a violation of the official oath of the office. Congressional qualifications are set exclusively by the U.S. Constitution, confirmed per https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R41946.html: "the Framers intended the Constitution to be the exclusive source of qualifications for Members of Congress, and that the Framers thereby 'divested' States of any power to add qualifications."

bio_summary.value: Brian Bengs grew up in a blue-collar family in rural northern Iowa. In high school he delivered newspapers every morning and detasseled corn in the summer. A member of his high school’s final graduating class, Brian enlisted in the U.S. Navy immediately after graduation. He first registered to vote (Independent) while assigned to the aircraft carrier USS Kitty Hawk (CV-63). At the end of his enlistment, he returned home and used the GI Bill to obtain a bachelor’s degree in history from Iowa State University where he met his wife of 30 years.

enacted_laws.title: RESPECT Act
enacted_laws.summary: Repealing Existing Substandard Provisions Encouraging Conciliation with Tribes Act or the RESPECT Act This act repeals certain provisions related to the treatment of Indians, including provisions on hostile tribes, alcohol, work requirements, penalties for truancy, and placement of youth in reform school without the consent of a parent or guardian.

bio_summary.value: Mike Rounds has a clear and solid record of serving the people of South Dakota. From growing up in Pierre as the oldest of eleven to building a small business and working as Governor, Mike has always stayed true to the values that make South Dakota special. Today, working as a United States Senator, he focuses on keeping South Dakota strong, growing opportunities for families and protecting the freedoms we all cherish.
